Pros & Cons can help when an urge feels urgent and its immediate payoff is crowding out longer-term consequences. The point is not to force a particular answer. The exercise compares both acting on the urge and resisting it by tolerating distress and choosing another response.

[Use the Pros & Cons tool](/tool-finder/pros-and-cons/){.btn .btn-primary}

## When Pros & Cons can help

Use it when:

- an urge is strong;
- acting immediately could create longer-term problems;
- part of you wants to act and another part wants to resist;
- consequences are hard to remember in the moment.

## Look at all four sides

Consider advantages and disadvantages for each option:

1. Pros of acting on the urge
2. Cons of acting on the urge
3. Pros of resisting the urge
4. Cons of resisting the urge

Looking at all four sides makes room for ambivalence. It also helps keep the exercise from becoming an argument for an answer chosen in advance.

## Short term and longer term

Something can feel helpful now while creating a cost later. Something can feel difficult now while supporting a longer-term goal. Notice what may happen today and what may matter beyond today without reducing the decision to a numerical score.

## Prepare before the urge is strongest

A completed list can be easier to use when it is prepared before distress is at its peak. When an urge becomes strong:

- review the list;
- remember what has happened after similar choices before;
- notice which consequences matter beyond the immediate moment;
- make the most mindful choice available.

#### Text Version

<!-- native-resource-content:distress-tolerance-p031:start -->

1. Describe the crisis behaviour or urge.
2. Examine the advantages and disadvantages of acting, then the advantages and disadvantages of resisting.
3. Consider both immediate and longer-term consequences.
4. Prepare separate lists for different urges when that is useful.
5. Review and rehearse the list before the urge is strongest.
6. Return to the list when the urge appears, and seek support when the situation calls for it.

<!-- native-resource-content:distress-tolerance-p031:end -->
